title: Partnership law firms can collapse even with zero debt and rising profits
dek: A 95-year-old Wall Street law firm with no major debt and rising profits collapsed within months like a bank run because its growth lagged competitors, proving partnerships fail from relative underperformance, not absolute financial decline.
why: The guest's academic papers predicted this collapse nearly point-by-point, concentrated on equity structure and bankruptcy mechanics rather than law firm gossip, densely argued and worth hearing in full.
who: Founders and investors focused on equity structure and partnership and employee-ownership models, plus people in eat-what-you-kill compensation systems at law firms, investment banks, and consulting firms.
skip: The opening chat about the host's personal impressions (roughly 0:00-4:00) is low-signal; jump straight to the formal interview.

points.h: Partnership law firms persist for historical and regulatory reasons, not efficiency
points.body: Partnership structures everywhere require partner ownership for three reasons. First, historically, starting a law practice required only labor, not capital. Second, state bar ethics rules mandate that lawyers own their firms. But the deeper explanation comes from Yale economist Henry Hansman: lawyers' output (billable hours traced to specific clients) is measurable in ways factory workers' output isn't, so partnerships create fewer internal profit-allocation disputes than worker ownership models. This measurability advantage is why Hansman's theory predicts partnerships over employee ownership schemes like at General Motors.

points.h: A key partner's departure triggers the run because costs don't fall with revenue
points.body: When a star partner leaves, clients follow almost immediately—revenue vanishes overnight. But office leases, pension obligations, and the salaries of junior partners who depended on that partner's client base don't shrink. If that partner was generating more revenue than his own compensation, his departure is pure loss. The profit pool that remaining partners split shrinks directly, forcing compensation cuts—and that's where the run begins.

points.h: Partner distributions become clawable at bankruptcy once the firm goes insolvent
points.body: Partners don't receive wages; they receive discretionary profit distributions, legally equivalent to dividends. Once a firm is declared insolvent, any further distributions to partners can be clawed back by creditors under fraudulent transfer law. This creates a calculation every partner silently runs: money in my pocket now might have to go back later.

points.h: Each partner constantly weighs leaving by expected value of compensation
points.body: Take a partner at Weil in September expecting $2 million in January. But if the firm has a 50% chance of collapsing by February, that $2 million is really worth only $1 million in expectation. If Gibson Dunn offers $1.5 million with lower failure risk, that's actually higher expected value—appearing to be a pay cut while genuinely being a raise. Every partner is quietly solving this problem. Once enough partners get the same answer, the run begins.

points.h: Falling in the rankings is more fatal than falling profits
points.body: Economist Morley's papers predicted exactly this scenario: a firm could collapse despite zero major debt and continued profit growth, provided growth lagged competitors. Weil's per-partner profit ranking fell from #9 in 2020 to #20 in 2025, while profits kept rising every year—just not as fast as Kirkland's. Weil got stuck: too small to be a megaplatform, too big to be a boutique like Wachtell or Cravath.

points.h: Partners' equity vanishes at retirement, so nobody invests for the future
points.body: A Microsoft shareholder can hold forever; future value gets priced into trading. A law firm partner's equity expires at retirement—no buyback, no perpetuity. This creates generational conflict: a 31-year-old partner might invest in the firm's future; a 61-year-old retiring in two years has zero incentive. This explains why law firms won't spend heavily to build AI systems that pay off in five years—because today's decision-makers won't be there to enjoy the returns.

points.h: Investor-owned law firms survive runs because partners aren't owners
points.body: Australian law firm Slater & Gordon is listed and investor-owned. Its Quindel acquisition turned out to be fraud, leaving the company insolvent. But because lawyers don't own the firm, management could wipe out shareholder equity and hand creditors the company as new shareholders in a restructuring—while lawyers kept their salaries and jobs, like Delta Airlines pilots. At a partnership like Weil, if you tried the same move, every partner walks to Cravath the next morning.

points.h: Law firms will lease AI like office space, not build it
points.body: Generational conflict means today's partners won't fund AI that pays off in five years, since different partners will be there then. Firms will license and rent AI technology like they lease offices—not own it like they'd buy a building. Kirkland & Ellis' $500 million AI program over five years looks ambitious until you note their ~$10 billion annual revenue—it's a rounding error, and they've paced it to sync with revenue growth, not to get ahead of it.
